Your perception surprises you

The Shepard tone, an endless staircase

A sound that seems to rise forever without ever getting higher. Cinema uses it to build tension.

In 1964, the psychologist Roger Shepard created a peculiar sound: several tones an octave apart play together and rise together. The highest fade out as new low ones fade in. The result sounds like a scale that keeps rising, although it actually always returns to the same point.

An auditory illusion

It is the sound equivalent of the impossible Penrose staircase or Escher's drawings. It works because we perceive not only a sound's frequency but also its "colour" within the octave, and the brain tracks the movement rather than the absolute pitch.

It has been used in music and film. The composer Hans Zimmer drew on it for the score of Dunkirk (2017) to sustain mounting tension throughout the film, and it appears in some video games on staircases that never end.

References

  1. Shepard, R. N. (1964). Circularity in judgments of relative pitch. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 36(12), 2346–2353.
  2. Deutsch, D. (2010). The paradox of pitch circularity. Acoustics Today, 6(3), 8–14.
